title: What is the 1-3-5 rule for ADHD, and does it work for cleaning?
description: The 1-3-5 rule for ADHD: one big task, three medium, five small per day. Where it comes from, why a capped list suits ADHD, and how to run it on a messy house.
h1: What is the 1-3-5 rule for ADHD? (and how to use it on a messy house)
target_query: what is the 1/3/5 rule for ADHD

faq.q: Does the 1-3-5 rule actually work for ADHD?
faq.a: There is no clinical trial of the 1-3-5 rule itself. What is well studied is the problem it works around: a long, unsorted list overloads working memory and stalls task initiation, and a short list with the size decided in advance removes both. So it works for the same reason a timer works. It is a container, not a treatment, and on a bad day even the five small ones count.

faq.q: What counts as a big, medium, or small task when cleaning?
faq.a: Size by time and by how many separate starts it needs, not by how important it feels. Big is 20 to 45 minutes and one zone: the kitchen reset, one doom pile sorted, the laundry cycle from basket to drawer. Medium is 5 to 15 minutes and one surface or one load: dishes, the coffee table, one bin bag round. Small is under 5 minutes and one object: cups walk, chair cleared, bathroom counter wiped.

faq.q: What if I only manage the five small tasks?
faq.a: Then you did the five small tasks, and the house is better than it was. The rule caps the day; it does not require the day to be full. Move the big one to tomorrow's slot and do not add anything to make up for it. On a low-energy day the small five alone are the whole plan.

faq.q: Is the 1-3-5 rule the same as the 1/3/5 rule?
faq.a: Yes. Same method, written with slashes or dashes depending on who is typing it. It comes from a 2013 productivity article by Alex Cavoulacos and was not designed for ADHD; it has been adopted because a fixed-size list happens to suit how an ADHD brain handles lists.

sources.supports: Working-memory limits in adult ADHD are why an open-ended to-do list overloads before anything gets started; a nine-item cap keeps the list inside what can be held.
Weak internal self-regulation is compensated by external structure; deciding task sizes the night before moves the sorting out of the moment.
Reduced dopamine reward signalling in ADHD is why five quick, visible completions matter more than one abstract big goal.
Time perception differences in ADHD are why tasks must be sized by measured minutes rather than by how long they feel.
